Rules summary Contents 1 Awkward Guests: The Walton Case 1.1 Goal 1.2 Information in the game 1.3 Round structure 1.4 Your turn 1.4.1 1. Inquiry Phase (ask for 2 references) 1.4.2 2. Offer Phase (others offer relevant cards) 1.4.3 3. Exchange Phase (you choose and pay) 1.5 End of the round 1.5.1 Solution Phase (everyone decides at once) 1.5.2 Discard Phase (if continuing) 1.6 If the game deck runs out 1.7 Useful rules for deduction 1.8 What the different card topics usually tell you 2 2-player differences 3 Solo mode Awkward Guests: The Walton Case This is a deduction and information-trading game. All players try to solve the murder on Mr. Walton. The first player to do so correctly, wins the game. Each player has their own investigation sheet (private to them) to keep track of the information they learn during the game. Goal Be the first player to correctly solve the case by identifying: - WHO killed Mr. Walton? - WHY did they kill him (motive)? - HOW did they put an end to his life (weapon)? - Was there an ACCOMPLICE and, if so, WHO and WHY ? (For Beginner / Very Easy / Easy cases there is never an accomplice.) Information in the game Each card has: - an information value (1–3), representing the amount of valuable information, and used to price exchanges; - references (suspects and/or rooms) showing what the info is about; - the case-related information; - how the information can be denoted on the tracking sheet. Round structure The game is played in rounds. In each round, every player takes one turn (anti-clockwise). Each turn has 3 phases: - Inquiry Phase - Offer Phase - Exchange Phase After all players have taken a turn, the round ends with a Solution Phase . If no one has solved the murder in this phase, the game continues with the Discard Phase . Your turn 1. Inquiry Phase (ask for 2 references) On your turn, you must request information about exactly 2 different references: - suspects (the 6 guests), and/or - rooms in the mansion. So you may ask for: 2 suspects, 2 rooms, or 1 suspect and 1 room. Arrows are used to show all players which 2 references have been chosen. 2. Offer Phase (others offer relevant cards) Starting with the player to your right and continuing anti-clockwise, each other player may prepare an offer: - They may offer any number of cards from their hand, or choose not to offer any cards at all; - Every offered card must contain at least one of the references you requested. - The offered cards are placed face down and a marker with the offer value (the sum of information values in the offer (1–3 per card)) is placed on top of it. Offers are final once declared. 3. Exchange Phase (you choose and pay) After all offers are made, you choose whether to exchange and with whom: - You may exchange with as many players as you want this turn; - For each chosen offer, give that player cards from your hand (any references allowed) totalling at least the offer value. - Exchanges are always for the full offered value. You cannot negotiate for part of an offer. All chosen exchanges are executed and players add received cards to their hands. If no one makes an offer, instead draw 3 cards (if possible), and your turn ends. End of the round Solution Phase (everyone decides at once) All players still in the game simultaneously choose: - Solve now, or - Continue investigating. Players who choose to solve determine their full accusation: - murderer; - motive; - weapon; - plus accomplice + accomplice motive (if they believe there is one). (Recall that for Beginner / Very Easy / Easy cases there is never an accomplice.) Then each solving player checks against the official solution (on BGA this is handled automatically, following the app rules). If a player is completely correct , the game ends and they win ; If a player is wrong , they are not eliminated. - As a penalty, that player is NOT allowed to participate in the Solution Phase of the next round. - Neither their guess nor the correct solution is revealed. Discard Phase (if continuing) All remaining players discard down to 3 cards in hand. Then the starting player marker passes to the player on the right, and the new starting player deals cards to refill everyone's hands back up to 6 cards (as far as possible). A new round begins. If the game deck runs out When the draw deck is empty: - The discard pile is shuffled to form a new deck; - The top 3 cards are revealed face up for everyone to examine, then placed into the revealed pile; - The rest of the pile is used as the new draw deck. Useful rules for deduction - The police/coroner/housekeeper/service staff do not lie. - The innocent guests do not lie regarding who they were with at the time of the murder. - The Berwick Sisters count as 2 guests but move and act as 1. What the different card topics usually tell you - Alibi info: where suspects claim to be at the time of the murder (only certain rooms are valid alibi rooms). If two suspects claim to be together (and vice versa), then either both are innocent, or they are the murderer and the accomplice. - Motive info: supports or dismisses possible motives. If all three motives of a suspect are dismissed, that suspect is innocent. - Conspiracy info: hints about possible accomplices. If there is an accomplice, staff will always find them conspiring, but some conspiracies can be red herrings. The accomplice only helps by giving an alibi (same room at murder time) and does not reveal the murderer's motive (and vice versa). - Weapon info: each weapon leaves two signs; missing either sign dismisses the weapon. The Study (crime scene) references often eliminate many weapons. - Opportunity/Movement info: who could reach the Study, and which rooms the murderer could have passed through. If a suspect cannot reach the Study via allowed routes, they cannot be the murderer. 2-player differences Play according to the rules above, with these changes: - Inquiry Phase: request information about 4 different references instead of 2 (any mix of suspects/rooms). - Exchange Phase: cards you receive are not kept. Both players look at received cards, take notes, then immediately discard them. - If the active player receives no offer, they draw 2 cards, take notes, then immediately discard those cards. Solo mode Play according to the rules above, with these changes: - Setup: You are assigned a starting score based on the difficulty level chosen. - Inquiry Phase: no change - Offer Phase: You will be offered up to 3 card/point combos related to the references chosen, and 1 card, worth 1 point, that is not restricted to the references. - Exchange Phase: Points will be deducted based on the offer chosen. Prior cards in hand will be discarded. - Solution Phase: An incorrect guess does not end the game, however it does disqualify you from guessing in the next round. - Goal: Find the correct solution with points remaining.

---

community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] Update :star::nostar::nostar::nostar::nostar:  Deck milling becomes annoying now. I really don't know why it's a thing, but there you go.   -----------------------  Average deduction game. The deck milling of evidence made the game very arbitrary. The choices on who to trade with is either obvious or engages in kingmaking.

[Rating: 1/10] Incómodos Invitados is the spanish version, looks like a good mix for my group, might be good, need to research.

[Rating: 2/10] Presold at price to a fellow gamer in Germany. Waiting for the game to arrive.  The game may be good, but the publishers are bad (terrible, uninformative communication, insisted on having the screen act at the same time as the sheet of paper that requires screening and then misprinted it), so, with so many games around, I don't feel like playing it any longer. So, according to the criteria of BGG this is a solid 2 to me.

[Rating: 2/10] Después de un segundo intento pude probar este juego. El primer intento fue imposible. El diminuto tamaño de la letra en algunos apartados de la hoja de anotaciones junto con la combinación de color sepia, hacía prácticamente imposible jugarlo.  En la segunda intentona, ya condicionada, negativamente, por lo comentado en el punto anterior, el dueño trajo unas lupas para subsanar este fallo de diseño.  Ni con este componente adicional salvó al juego de ser divertido. Fue una hora y cuarto de total aburrimiento, pasas cartas, te dan cartas y te vuelven a venir pistas que ya tenías antes. Mención

[Rating: 2/10] Difficult to set up and time-consuming to put away. Overly complicated Cluedo-like game.

[Rating: 2/10] theme is cool, there is barely any deduction at perfect crime. Just waiting for right cards, there is no game

[Rating: 2/10] Tenía muchas ganas de que me gustara, pero no fue así. Jugamos una partida "muy fácil" y fue compleja y extremadamente larga. Todavía no entiendo que implica la coletilla de un sospechoso "que puede haber visto". Sobrevalorado. El arte western tampoco me entusiasma. Pérdida de dinero

[Rating: 2.5/10] Sorry...the game doesn’t truly play the way it is marketed.  There is deduction in the Character/murderer, some deduction in the weapon (but is usually the most described in the deck and easiest for all to determine) and no deduction in the motive.  Basically, you pass the same cards around for an hour until there is a reshuffle, then you wait for somebody to see the 4 cards that are absolutely needed to determine the answer...I will stick with Sleuth.
